result:
The morning light hit the kitchen counter at an angle that made the dust visible, each particle suspended in its own slow orbit, and I thought about how we are all just dust that learned to complain. My grandmother's ceramic rooster watched from the windowsill, beak eternally open in a crow he would never finish. She bought it in 1987 from a man who swore it was hand-painted in Portugal. It was made in Ohio. The lie outlived her.

I've been thinking about the physics of regret. How it doesn't dissipate like heat but accumulates, mass without volume, until you're carrying a black hole in your ribcage that weighs precisely nothing and everything. Last Tuesday I saw a man at the bus stop reading a manual for a refrigerator he'd owned for twelve years. "Finally getting around to it," he said, though I hadn't asked. The manual was in German. He didn't speak German. This is what we do with instructions we never requested.

My neighbor waters her concrete driveway every evening at six. She believes this prevents cracks. The water runs into the street, down the grate, joins the river, the ocean, the clouds, falls again on some other driveway where someone else stands with a hose, believing they are holding back entropy with a green rubber grip. We are all Sisyphus but with worse posture and no mythic significance.

The word "sillage" refers to the scent-trail left by perfume. I learned this from a woman who left my apartment at 4 AM and took all the warmth with her. For weeks I would enter rooms and still smell her decision to go. The dictionary calls it a wake, like behind a boat, like after a death. We have so few words for departure that we must recycle them until they mean everything and nothing, like "love" or "okay" or "I'm fine."

Children are born with about 100 more bones than adults have. They fuse, ossify, become rigid with time. We are born flexible and spend our lives becoming architecture. I think about this when I see toddlers fold themselves into spaces that shouldn't accommodate them, when I try to touch my toes and my body sends back a polite refusal, a returned letter, address unknown.

There is a town in Japan where they make fake food for restaurant displays. The craftsmen study real food for hours, then reproduce it in resin and wax. The shrimp tempura will never cool. The lettuce will never wilt. The perfect meal, eternally almost-ready. I want to ask them if they dream of hunger, if the imitation of satisfaction becomes its own kind of nourishment. I never go to Japan. I look at pictures online and feel approximately informed.

My father kept a list of every book he read from 1974 to 2003. The handwriting changed, tightened, then loosened again when arthritis arrived. Somewhere around 1987 the titles stop being things he chose and start being things assigned, recommended, expected. You can see the exact moment he stopped reading for pleasure and started reading for proof that he was still the kind of person who read. The list ends mid-page. I don't know if he stopped keeping it or stopped reading or just stopped needing evidence.

The Voyager golden record contains a heartbeat. Ann Druyan's, recorded while she thought about Carl Sagan, whom she would later marry. The sound of love traveling at 35,000 miles per hour toward stars that may have already died, carrying Bach and Chuck Berry and the hope that something, somewhere, will know what a heartbeat means. We are so desperate to be understood that we launched our longing into the dark with no address, no return postage, just the assumption that beauty is a language with no need for translation.

I used to think nostalgia was a weakness. Now I think it's a survival mechanism, the brain's way of saying *this mattered* when the present insists nothing matters yet. The smell of chalkboards. The particular green of library card catalogues. The weight of a phone receiver in the crook of your neck, cord stretched to its limit so you could stand in the doorway and watch rain while someone you would eventually lose told you about their day. These details are not important. They are everything.

The last person who knew how to make Stradivari's varnish died without explaining it. We have his instruments, their sound, their impossible resonance, but not the recipe. Some knowledge travels only through bodies, dies with them, becomes archaeology of the air. I wonder what I know that I cannot explain, what will vanish when I do, what small craft I perform without understanding its mechanics, its worth.

At the hospital where I was born, they now use that wing for storage. Boxes of files no one will request. The room where my mother first held me holds fluorescent light and the smell of old paper. I want to visit it but they don't allow visitors to storage. The building remembers nothing. The building doesn't need to. The building is still standing, which is its own kind of memory, its own indifferent continuity.

I read that sharks have to keep moving to breathe. The water flows through, extracts oxygen, requires motion. To stop is to suffocate. I think about this when I can't sleep, when I scroll through feeds I don't care about, when I answer "busy" to "how are you" because stillness feels like drowning. We are all sharks in a tank too small, circling, circling, telling ourselves the motion is the point.

The word "petrichor" was invented in 1964 by two scientists who studied the smell of rain on dry earth. Before that, we had the experience but not the name. How many things do we feel that remain unnamed because the right two people haven't collaborated yet? The particular ache of seeing someone you used to know in a crowd and choosing not to say hello. The way a house sounds different when you know you're leaving it. The exact color of the light at the moment you realize you are older than your parents were when they had you.

I keep a box of letters I will never send. The recipients are scattered, dead, estranged, or simply uninterested in my versions of events. The letters grow more accurate with time, less concerned with persuasion, more with record. This is what I saw. This is what I failed to say. This is how I remember it, which is not how it was, but how it remains in the only archive I have, this faulty, loving, self-serving mind.

The oldest known melody was written on a cuneiform tablet in Syria, fourteen centuries before the common era. It was for a stringed instrument, maybe a lyre. The notation is partly understood. We can play something close to what they played, but not exact, never exact, the gap between then and now unbridgeable by any music. Still, someone plays it. Someone always plays it. The approximation of connection is itself a kind of connection, the reaching across time with imperfect hands, saying *I hear you, or something like you, or what I imagine you might have been.*

My cat sleeps sixteen hours a day and wakes without apology, without the need to justify her existence through productivity. I have never envied anything more completely. The moral of evolution is not progress but adaptation, and she has adapted to a world that provides, that asks nothing in return but presence, the occasional purr, the acknowledgment that warmth is enough, that enough is rare and sufficient.

I am running out of words now, which is the condition of all things, the built-in limit that makes them precious. The ceramic rooster still waits. The bus stop man has probably finished his manual, understood nothing, moved on to another project of incomprehension. The fake food glows in Tokyo windows. Voyager passes the edge of our influence, still singing its heart into the void. And somewhere it is raining on dry earth, making a smell that didn't have a name within my grandmother's lifetime, making it anyway, making it new each time, indifferent to whether we have words, whether we are watching, whether we will remember to move, to breathe, to continue this impossible, ordinary, sufficient motion of being alive.
